title: Class 2: More servos, more personalities

series.title: Physical AI Lab: Build a Robot Desk Assistant (4 evenings)

summary: Give your robot's servos their own power, add two moving eyes, and give it several personalities you can switch between by voice: "let me talk to the Tooth Fairy". The laptop stays the brain tonight.
detail: Bring your robot from Evening 1. First the servos get their own power supply, so adding more doesn't reset the Pico: a breadboard fed by a phone charger, or a BreadVolt battery module if you bought one. Then the eyes: two eyeballs on two small servos, from the group order. The robot program on your Pico already knows how to drive them. Tick My robot has moving eyes on this page and your robot can cross its eyes or look left and right when you ask, and its eyes glance around while it talks. The second half is all voice studio: build more personalities, each with its own name, voice and first line, and switch between them mid-conversation. Asking it to cross its eyes is your first function call, a taste of Evening 3.
outcome: A robot with moving eyes on their own power supply, and several personalities you swap by voice.
artifact: A talking robot with moving eyes and switchable personalities.
prereqs: Your robot from Evening 1, with its Pico.
Your laptop with Google Chrome, and your Deepgram API key.
Power for the servos, your choice: a USB charger with the flat USB-A port (an old phone charger is perfect; we have a few spares), or a SunFounder BreadVolt (about $10) for battery power.
Eye servos: 2 per person, from the group order in Evening 1. We bring the eyeballs and the breadboards.

slides.title: Class 2: More servos, more personalities
bullets: First half: the servos get their own power, and your robot gets eyes.
Second half: more personalities, and switching between them by voice.
The laptop stays the brain tonight.
slides.note: Show a robot with moving eyes switching personality at the start, so people know where the evening goes.

slides.title: What each robot needs today
bullets: ☐ Your robot from Evening 1, with its Pico
☐ 1 × half-size breadboard with + and − rails (on the table; already have one from Evening 1? keep it)
Power, one of: ☐ USB-to-2-pin power lead + a USB-A charger, or ☐ your BreadVolt, set to 5 V
☐ 1 × male-to-male jumper (ground to the Pico)
Eyes: ☐ 2 × eyeballs ☐ 2 × MG90S servos with horns ☐ 2 × male-to-female jumpers (signal) ☐ 4 × male-to-male jumpers (power)
☐ Glue gun (one per table, with a helper nearby)
Bring: your laptop and your Deepgram key
slides.note: Dana brings the eyeballs. The eye servos come from the group order placed after Evening 1: hand out 2 per person from the chip-in list. Pre-bag the eye kits so people grab one and go. Every Pico already runs the program with eyes support, so nobody reloads anything. Helper table: spare USB-A chargers, USB-C to USB-A adapters, a power strip per table, spare 2-pin leads.

slides.title: Give the servos their own power
bullets: Take the mouth's red off pin 40 and brown off pin 38.
Red → breadboard + row, brown → − row.
One jumper from the − row to GND (pin 23): everything shares one ground.
Feed the rows: the 2-pin lead into a charger (red pin → +, black → −), or press your BreadVolt onto the rails and switch it on.
Nothing on pin 40 from now on. Plug the Pico back into the laptop.
slides.note: Anyone who hit resets in Evening 1 is already wired this way: they skip to the eyes. Check the BreadVolt's jumpers are on 5 V, not 3.3 V. Connected but the mouth won't move = the servo has no power: the BreadVolt is switched off or the lead isn't in a charger.

slides.title: Mount the eyes
bullets: Cut two holes in the face, above the mouth, just big enough for the eyeballs.
Glue each eyeball to the top of a servo horn, then push the horn onto its servo.
From inside, glue each servo behind its hole so the eyeball sits in the hole and can turn left and right.
Turn each eyeball gently by hand: it should swing freely.
slides.note: Check this against the eyeballs Dana brings and adjust the hole size. Done when: both eyes turn freely by hand without catching the face.

slides.title: Wire the eyes
bullets: Left eye's orange wire to GP13 (pin 17), right eye's to GP12 (pin 16), with male-to-female jumpers.
Both reds to the + row, both browns to the − row, like the mouth.
Nothing new goes on the Pico's power pins.
Plug the Pico back into your laptop.
slides.note: Left and right mean the robot's left and right, as if you were the robot. Pins 16 and 17 are on the left side, just above GP14 (pin 19) and GP15 (pin 20). Helpers check every board before it's plugged in.

slides.title: Switch them on
bullets: Connect the robot, then open Eyes under Plug in your robot.
Tick My robot has moving eyes.
Press Cross eyes, Look left and Look right to test.
Start talking and ask it to cross its eyes. Watch the Tool line: that's a function call moving real hardware.
slides.note: If they cross outward, swap the two eye wires (GP12 and GP13). The eyes switch off when the robot is quiet, so they don't buzz. If nothing moves at all, the Pico has the old program: load the current one at the helper table.

slides.title: A robot with more than one personality
bullets: Under Profile, press Add a profile: start from a starter (like Arnie) or a blank one.
Give it a Robot name, a Personality, a First thing it says and its own Voice.
Make them as different as you can: grumpy and cheerful, fast and slow, a pirate and a tooth fairy.
Start talking and say: let me talk to the Tooth Fairy (or whatever you named it). It changes voice and personality on the spot.
slides.note: Switching works because the agent understands what you asked for and calls switch_profile; the page swaps the personality and voice live, without hanging up. So any natural phrasing works: "switch to Arnie", "put the pirate on". Remove this profile deletes the one you're on, so check before pressing.

slides.title: Make them hand off to each other
bullets: In each personality, say who else lives in the robot and when to hand over.
Example: "If someone asks about teeth, offer to get the Tooth Fairy."
Try a three-way: start with one, get passed to a second, ask for the first back.
Keep each one's replies short so the switches feel quick.
slides.note: Good pairs to suggest: a grumpy security guard and a cheerful receptionist; a pirate captain and a parrot; a coach and a nervous rookie.

slides.title: You just used a function call
bullets: "Cross your eyes" and "let me talk to the Tooth Fairy" are both function calls.
The agent decides it needs one, your page runs it, and real hardware (or a new voice) answers.
Next evening your robot gets skills the same way: the bus, timers, notes, look-ups, the weather.
slides.note: Point at the Tool lines in the transcript while a robot crosses its eyes. That's the whole idea of Evening 3.

slides.title: Meet the neighbours
bullets: Turn to the next table and introduce your robot.
Let each of its personalities introduce itself.
Film a clip with Film a clip and share it with #RobotLunchLab.

slides.title: Evening 3: skills, and cut the cord
bullets: Your robot gets skills: real function calls with real data.
And it gets off the laptop. Android phone? Use Chrome. iPhone? Download the free Bluefy app before you come.
Your phone becomes the robot's brain over Bluetooth, and the robot sits on a charger or BreadVolt.
Want it all inside the box? Bring a Raspberry Pi set up at home. The steps are on the Evening 3 page.
Study hall: every Tuesday from 11 AM until class. Drop in any time: snacks, decorating, upgrades, and catch-up if you missed an evening.
slides.note: Bluetooth works on Android (tested: about 50 ms from phone to mouth). iPhone with Bluefy is still being tested, and nobody has run 50 robots on Bluetooth in one room yet: pitch that as part of the fun. Send the Evening 3 page to anyone thinking about a Pi now, so they set it up at home.

troubleshooting: Connected but the mouth won't move: the servos have no power. Switch the BreadVolt on, or plug the 2-pin lead into a charger.
Your charger is USB-C only: the 2-pin lead is USB-A. Use a USB-C to USB-A adapter from the helper table, or a table charger.

The eyes don't move at all: check the orange wires are on GP13 (pin 17) and GP12 (pin 16), and the reds and browns are on the + and − rows. Still nothing? The Pico has an old program: load the current one at the helper table.
The eyes cross outward: swap the left and right eye wires.
Left and right are backwards: swap the two eye wires.
An eye catches on the face: make the hole a little bigger, or move the servo back.
The servos twitch on their own: the ground jumper from the − row to pin 23 is missing.

The page says the robot reset while talking: a servo is pulling power from the Pico. Check every red wire goes to the + row, the BreadVolt is switched on or the power lead is in a charger, nothing is on pin 40, and the ground jumper to pin 23 is in.
It won't switch personality: say the profile's Robot name clearly, and check the profile has a name.
Connect robot does nothing at all: you're not in Chrome. Open the page in Chrome (or Chromium on a Raspberry Pi).
Another program is using the port: quit Thonny and close other tabs with this page, unplug the Pico, plug it back in, and connect again.
It cuts you off: raise Patience. It's slow to answer: lower it.
It talks to itself, or stops mid-sentence for no reason: it's hearing its own voice. Switch off Let me interrupt it (barge-in), or move the laptop away from the robot's speaker.
Deepgram stopped the session: check the key was pasted whole, and that the account has credit.
